Real Analysis — 01 · Sequences and Series

Created2026-03-13|Updated2026-03-13|Mathematics > Real Analysis
|Post View:

A sequence is the simplest infinite process in mathematics, and its limit is the idea on which the rest of analysis is built: derivatives, integrals and continuity are all limits in disguise. This post makes "the terms get closer and closer to aaa" precise with the ε\varepsilonε–NNN definition, works through explicit proofs with concrete numbers, and then proves the big structural theorems that rest on the completeness of R\mathbb{R}R from Real Analysis 00: the Monotone Convergence Theorem, Bolzano–Weierstrass and the Cauchy criterion. The second half turns to infinite series — sums of infinitely many numbers — with the standard convergence tests and the surprising fact that reordering the terms of some series changes the sum.

Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness → 01 Sequences & Series (this post) → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem → 04 The Riemann Integral → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series.

Learning Outcome

  • State the ε\varepsilonε–NNN definition of convergence and write complete proofs that specific sequences converge, with an explicit NNN.
  • Prove that limits are unique and that convergent sequences are bounded.
  • Prove the sum and product parts of the Algebraic Limit Theorem, and use the Order Limit Theorem and the squeeze theorem.
  • Prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem and apply it to a recursively defined sequence.
  • Prove the Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem by bisection and use subsequences to show divergence.
  • Define Cauchy sequences, lim sup⁡\limsuplimsup and lim inf⁡\liminfliminf, and state the Cauchy criterion.
  • Decide convergence of series with the divergence, comparison, ratio, root and alternating series tests.
  • Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence and state the Riemann rearrangement theorem.

Chapter 1 — The limit of a sequence

Terminology

  • Sequence — a function from N\mathbb{N}N to R\mathbb{R}R, written (an)=(a1,a2,a3,… )(a_n) = (a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots)(an​)=(a1​,a2​,a3​,…).
  • ε\varepsilonε-neighbourhood of aaa — the interval Vε(a)=(a−ε,a+ε)V_\varepsilon(a) = (a - \varepsilon, a + \varepsilon)Vε​(a)=(a−ε,a+ε), the points within distance ε\varepsilonε of aaa.
  • Converges — (an)(a_n)(an​) converges to aaa, written an→aa_n \to aan​→a or lim⁡an=a\lim a_n = aliman​=a, if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is N∈NN \in \mathbb{N}N∈N such that ∣an−a∣<ε\lvert a_n - a \rvert < \varepsilon∣an​−a∣<ε for all n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N.
  • Diverges — does not converge to any real number.
  • Tail — the terms aN,aN+1,…a_N, a_{N+1}, \dotsaN​,aN+1​,… from some index on.
  • Bounded — there is M>0M > 0M>0 with ∣an∣≤M\lvert a_n \rvert \le M∣an​∣≤M for all nnn.

The definition says: whatever tolerance ε\varepsilonε is demanded, the whole tail from some NNN on lies inside the band Vε(a)V_\varepsilon(a)Vε​(a). The NNN is allowed to depend on ε\varepsilonε (a smaller band usually needs a larger NNN). Finitely many early terms never matter.

Uniqueness and boundedness

Theorem. A sequence has at most one limit.

Proof. Suppose an→aa_n \to aan​→a and an→ba_n \to ban​→b. Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. There are N1,N2N_1, N_2N1​,N2​ with ∣an−a∣<ε/2\lvert a_n - a \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣an​−a∣<ε/2 for n≥N1n \ge N_1n≥N1​ and ∣an−b∣<ε/2\lvert a_n - b \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣an​−b∣<ε/2 for n≥N2n \ge N_2n≥N2​. For n=max⁡(N1,N2)n = \max(N_1, N_2)n=max(N1​,N2​),

∣a−b∣≤∣a−an∣+∣an−b∣<ε.\lvert a - b \rvert \le \lvert a - a_n \rvert + \lvert a_n - b \rvert < \varepsilon. ∣a−b∣≤∣a−an​∣+∣an​−b∣<ε.

Since ε\varepsilonε was arbitrary, a=ba = ba=b by the equality lemma of Real Analysis 00. ■\blacksquare■

Theorem. Every convergent sequence is bounded.

Proof. Let an→aa_n \to aan​→a. With ε=1\varepsilon = 1ε=1 there is NNN such that ∣an−a∣<1\lvert a_n - a \rvert < 1∣an​−a∣<1, hence ∣an∣<∣a∣+1\lvert a_n \rvert < \lvert a \rvert + 1∣an​∣<∣a∣+1, for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N. Put M=max⁡{∣a1∣,…,∣aN−1∣,∣a∣+1}M = \max\{\lvert a_1 \rvert, \dots, \lvert a_{N-1} \rvert, \lvert a \rvert + 1\}M=max{∣a1​∣,…,∣aN−1​∣,∣a∣+1}. Then ∣an∣≤M\lvert a_n \rvert \le M∣an​∣≤M for all nnn. ■\blacksquare■

The converse is false: (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n is bounded and divergent.

Common pitfall: choosing NNN that depends on nnn. In "∀ε ∃N ∀n≥N\forall \varepsilon\ \exists N\ \forall n \ge N∀ε ∃N ∀n≥N" the order says NNN is chosen after ε\varepsilonε but before nnn. "Take N=n+1N = n + 1N=n+1" is not a proof.

The Algebraic Limit Theorem

Theorem. Let an→aa_n \to aan​→a and bn→bb_n \to bbn​→b. Then
(i) c an→c ac\,a_n \to c\,acan​→ca for every c∈Rc \in \mathbb{R}c∈R;
(ii) an+bn→a+ba_n + b_n \to a + ban​+bn​→a+b;
(iii) anbn→aba_n b_n \to aban​bn​→ab;
(iv) an/bn→a/ba_n / b_n \to a / ban​/bn​→a/b, provided b≠0b \ne 0b=0 (and bn≠0b_n \ne 0bn​=0 for all nnn).

Proof of (ii). Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Choose N1N_1N1​ with ∣an−a∣<ε/2\lvert a_n - a \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣an​−a∣<ε/2 for n≥N1n \ge N_1n≥N1​, and N2N_2N2​ with ∣bn−b∣<ε/2\lvert b_n - b \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣bn​−b∣<ε/2 for n≥N2n \ge N_2n≥N2​. For n≥max⁡(N1,N2)n \ge \max(N_1, N_2)n≥max(N1​,N2​),

∣(an+bn)−(a+b)∣≤∣an−a∣+∣bn−b∣<ε2+ε2=ε.■\lvert (a_n + b_n) - (a + b) \rvert \le \lvert a_n - a \rvert + \lvert b_n - b \rvert < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare ∣(an​+bn​)−(a+b)∣≤∣an​−a∣+∣bn​−b∣<2ε​+2ε​=ε.■

Proof of (iii). Add and subtract anba_n ban​b:

∣anbn−ab∣=∣an(bn−b)+(an−a)b∣≤∣an∣∣bn−b∣+∣b∣∣an−a∣.\lvert a_n b_n - ab \rvert = \lvert a_n (b_n - b) + (a_n - a) b \rvert \le \lvert a_n \rvert \lvert b_n - b \rvert + \lvert b \rvert \lvert a_n - a \rvert. ∣an​bn​−ab∣=∣an​(bn​−b)+(an​−a)b∣≤∣an​∣∣bn​−b∣+∣b∣∣an​−a∣.

(an)(a_n)(an​) converges, so it is bounded: ∣an∣≤M\lvert a_n \rvert \le M∣an​∣≤M for some M>0M > 0M>0. Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. (The +1+1+1 avoids dividing by zero when b=0b = 0b=0.) For n≥max⁡(N1,N2)n \ge \max(N_1, N_2)n≥max(N1​,N2​),

∣anbn−ab∣<M⋅ε2M+∣b∣⋅ε2(∣b∣+1)<ε2+ε2=ε.■\lvert a_n b_n - ab \rvert < M \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2M} + \lvert b \rvert \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2(\lvert b \rvert + 1)} < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare ∣an​bn​−ab∣<M⋅2Mε​+∣b∣⋅2(∣b∣+1)ε​<2ε​+2ε​=ε.■

Order and squeezing

Order Limit Theorem. Let an→aa_n \to aan​→a and bn→bb_n \to bbn​→b.
(i) If an≥0a_n \ge 0an​≥0 for all nnn, then a≥0a \ge 0a≥0.
(ii) If an≤bna_n \le b_nan​≤bn​ for all nnn, then a≤ba \le ba≤b.
(iii) If c≤bnc \le b_nc≤bn​ for all nnn, then c≤bc \le bc≤b; if an≤ca_n \le can​≤c for all nnn, then a≤ca \le ca≤c.

Proof of (i). Suppose a<0a < 0a<0. Take ε=∣a∣\varepsilon = \lvert a \rvertε=∣a∣. For large nnn, ∣an−a∣<∣a∣\lvert a_n - a \rvert < \lvert a \rvert∣an​−a∣<∣a∣, which gives an<a+∣a∣=0a_n < a + \lvert a \rvert = 0an​<a+∣a∣=0, a contradiction. Part (ii) is (i) applied to bn−anb_n - a_nbn​−an​, and (iii) is (ii) with a constant sequence. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: strict inequalities are not preserved. 1/n>01/n > 01/n>0 for every nnn, but lim⁡1/n=0\lim 1/n = 0lim1/n=0. Limits turn <<< into ≤\le≤.

Squeeze theorem. If xn≤yn≤znx_n \le y_n \le z_nxn​≤yn​≤zn​ for all nnn and xn→ℓx_n \to \ellxn​→ℓ, zn→ℓz_n \to \ellzn​→ℓ, then yn→ℓy_n \to \ellyn​→ℓ. Example: 0≤∣sin⁡n∣n≤1n0 \le \frac{\lvert\sin n\rvert}{n} \le \frac1n0≤n∣sinn∣​≤n1​, so sin⁡nn→0\frac{\sin n}{n} \to 0nsinn​→0.

Chapter 3 — Monotone sequences

Terminology

  • Increasing — an≤an+1a_n \le a_{n+1}an​≤an+1​ for all nnn. Decreasing — an≥an+1a_n \ge a_{n+1}an​≥an+1​ for all nnn.
  • Monotone — increasing or decreasing.

The Monotone Convergence Theorem

Theorem. A monotone sequence converges if and only if it is bounded. An increasing bounded sequence converges to sup⁡{an:n∈N}\sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}sup{an​:n∈N}.

Proof. Convergent implies bounded (Chapter 1). Conversely, let (an)(a_n)(an​) be increasing and bounded. The set {an}\{a_n\}{an​} is nonempty and bounded above, so by the Axiom of Completeness s=sup⁡{an}s = \sup\{a_n\}s=sup{an​} exists. Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Since s−εs - \varepsilons−ε is not an upper bound, some aN>s−εa_N > s - \varepsilonaN​>s−ε. For n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N, monotonicity and sss being an upper bound give

s−ε<aN≤an≤s,s - \varepsilon < a_N \le a_n \le s, s−ε<aN​≤an​≤s,

so ∣an−s∣<ε\lvert a_n - s \rvert < \varepsilon∣an​−s∣<ε. The decreasing case is the same with the infimum. ■\blacksquare■

The theorem proves that a limit exists without knowing its value in advance — the essential use of completeness. In Q\mathbb{Q}Q it fails: the increasing bounded sequence 1,1.4,1.41,1.414,…1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \dots1,1.4,1.41,1.414,… of decimal truncations of 2\sqrt{2}2​ has no rational limit.

Chapter 4 — Subsequences, Bolzano–Weierstrass and Cauchy sequences

Terminology

  • Subsequence of (an)(a_n)(an​) — a sequence (ank)=(an1,an2,… )(a_{n_k}) = (a_{n_1}, a_{n_2}, \dots)(ank​​)=(an1​​,an2​​,…) with n1<n2<n3<⋯n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdotsn1​<n2​<n3​<⋯. It keeps infinitely many terms, in order.
  • Cauchy sequence — for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is NNN such that ∣an−am∣<ε\lvert a_n - a_m \rvert < \varepsilon∣an​−am​∣<ε for all m,n≥Nm, n \ge Nm,n≥N. The terms get close to each other, with no limit mentioned.
  • Limit superior — lim sup⁡an=lim⁡n→∞yn\limsup a_n = \lim_{n \to \infty} y_nlimsupan​=limn→∞​yn​ where yn=sup⁡{ak:k≥n}y_n = \sup\{a_k : k \ge n\}yn​=sup{ak​:k≥n}. Limit inferior — the same with inf⁡\infinf.

Theorem. If an→aa_n \to aan​→a, every subsequence also converges to aaa. (Given ε\varepsilonε and NNN for (an)(a_n)(an​), use the same NNN: nk≥kn_k \ge knk​≥k, so k≥Nk \ge Nk≥N implies nk≥Nn_k \ge Nnk​≥N.)

This gives the quickest divergence proofs: find two subsequences with different limits. For (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n, the even terms tend to 111 and the odd terms to −1-1−1.

Bolzano–Weierstrass

Theorem (Bolzano–Weierstrass). Every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence.

Proof (bisection). Let ∣an∣≤M\lvert a_n \rvert \le M∣an​∣≤M and I1=[−M,M]I_1 = [-M, M]I1​=[−M,M]. Choose n1=1n_1 = 1n1​=1. Split I1I_1I1​ into two closed halves; at least one contains ana_nan​ for infinitely many nnn. Call it I2I_2I2​ and choose n2>n1n_2 > n_1n2​>n1​ with an2∈I2a_{n_2} \in I_2an2​​∈I2​. The Cauchy criterion

Theorem (Cauchy criterion). A sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.

Proof. (⇒\Rightarrow⇒) If an→aa_n \to aan​→a, choose NNN with ∣an−a∣<ε/2\lvert a_n - a \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣an​−a∣<ε/2 for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N. For m,n≥Nm, n \ge Nm,n≥N, ∣an−am∣≤∣an−a∣+∣a−am∣<ε\lvert a_n - a_m \rvert \le \lvert a_n - a \rvert + \lvert a - a_m \rvert < \varepsilon∣an​−am​∣≤∣an​−a∣+∣a−am​∣<ε.

(⇐\Leftarrow⇐) Let (an)(a_n)(an​) be Cauchy.
Bounded: with ε=1\varepsilon = 1ε=1 there is NNN with ∣an−aN∣<1\lvert a_n - a_N \rvert < 1∣an​−aN​∣<1 for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N, so ∣an∣<∣aN∣+1\lvert a_n \rvert < \lvert a_N \rvert + 1∣an​∣<∣aN​∣+1 for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N; take the maximum with the first N−1N - 1N−1 terms.
A subsequence converges: by Bolzano–Weierstrass, ank→aa_{n_k} \to aank​​→a for some aaa.
The whole sequence follows: given ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, choose NNN with ∣an−am∣<ε/2\lvert a_n - a_m \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣an​−am​∣<ε/2 for m,n≥Nm, n \ge Nm,n≥N, and choose kkk with nk≥Nn_k \ge Nnk​≥N and ∣ank−a∣<ε/2\lvert a_{n_k} - a \rvert < \varepsilon/2∣ank​​−a∣<ε/2. For n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N,

∣an−a∣≤∣an−ank∣+∣ank−a∣<ε.■\lvert a_n - a \rvert \le \lvert a_n - a_{n_k} \rvert + \lvert a_{n_k} - a \rvert < \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare ∣an​−a∣≤∣an​−ank​​∣+∣ank​​−a∣<ε.■

The Cauchy criterion lets you prove convergence using only the terms themselves. In Q\mathbb{Q}Q it fails: the Newton sequence of Chapter 3 is a Cauchy sequence of rationals with no rational limit. Completeness of R\mathbb{R}R can be defined by "every Cauchy sequence converges" together with the Archimedean property; it is equivalent to the Axiom of Completeness.

Watch out: "consecutive terms get close" is not the Cauchy condition. For an=na_n = \sqrt{n}an​=n​, an+1−an=1n+1+n→0a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+1} + \sqrt{n}} \to 0an+1​−an​=n+1​+n​1​→0, yet an→∞a_n \to \inftyan​→∞. Cauchy requires ∣an−am∣\lvert a_n - a_m \rvert∣an​−am​∣ small for all pairs m,n≥Nm, n \ge Nm,n≥N.

Limit superior and inferior

For a bounded sequence, yn=sup⁡{ak:k≥n}y_n = \sup\{a_k : k \ge n\}yn​=sup{ak​:k≥n} is decreasing (a supremum over a smaller set) and bounded, so lim sup⁡an=lim⁡yn\limsup a_n = \lim y_nlimsupan​=limyn​ always exists by the Monotone Convergence Theorem; likewise lim inf⁡\liminfliminf. Always lim inf⁡an≤lim sup⁡an\liminf a_n \le \limsup a_nliminfan​≤limsupan​.

Example. an=(−1)n(1+1n)a_n = (-1)^n\left(1 + \frac1n\right)an​=(−1)n(1+n1​): the terms are −2,32,−43,54,…-2, \tfrac32, -\tfrac43, \tfrac54, \dots−2,23​,−34​,45​,…. The even terms decrease to 111 and the odd terms increase to −1-1−1, so lim sup⁡an=1\limsup a_n = 1limsupan​=1 and lim inf⁡an=−1\liminf a_n = -1liminfan​=−1, although no term equals 111 or −1-1−1.

Theorem. A bounded sequence converges if and only if lim inf⁡an=lim sup⁡an\liminf a_n = \limsup a_nliminfan​=limsupan​, and then the limit is this common value.

lim sup⁡\limsuplimsup is the largest limit of any subsequence and lim inf⁡\liminfliminf the smallest. These notions give the sharp form of the root test in Chapter 6.

Chapter 5 — Infinite series

Terminology

  • Series — an expression ∑k=1∞ak\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k∑k=1∞​ak​. Its partial sums are sn=a1+a2+⋯+ans_n = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_nsn​=a1​+a2​+⋯+an​.
  • Converges — the sequence (sn)(s_n)(sn​) converges; its limit SSS is the sum, written ∑k=1∞ak=S\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k = S∑k=1∞​ak​=S.
  • Diverges — (sn)(s_n)(sn​) does not converge.

A series is a sequence in disguise: every question about ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ is a question about (sn)(s_n)(sn​).

Geometric and telescoping series

Geometric series. For r≠1r \ne 1r=1, sn=∑k=0n−1rk=1−rn1−rs_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k = \frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r}sn​=∑k=0n−1​rk=1−r1−rn​ (multiply by 1−r1 - r1−r and cancel). If ∣r∣<1\lvert r \rvert < 1∣r∣<1, then rn→0r^n \to 0rn→0 and

∑k=0∞rk=11−r.\sum_{k=0}^\infty r^k = \frac{1}{1 - r}. k=0∑∞​rk=1−r1​.

If ∣r∣≥1\lvert r \rvert \ge 1∣r∣≥1 the series diverges (its terms do not tend to 000). Example: ∑k=1∞(12)k=11−1/2−1=1\sum_{k=1}^\infty \left(\tfrac12\right)^k = \frac{1}{1 - 1/2} - 1 = 1∑k=1∞​(21​)k=1−1/21​−1=1.

Telescoping series. 1k(k+1)=1k−1k+1\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac1k - \frac{1}{k+1}k(k+1)1​=k1​−k+11​, so the partial sums collapse: sn=1−1n+1→1s_n = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1} \to 1sn​=1−n+11​→1. Hence ∑k=1∞1k(k+1)=1\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k(k+1)} = 1∑k=1∞​k(k+1)1​=1.

The divergence test

Theorem. If ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges, then ak→0a_k \to 0ak​→0.

Proof. ak=sk−sk−1a_k = s_k - s_{k-1}ak​=sk​−sk−1​, and both sks_ksk​ and sk−1s_{k-1}sk−1​ tend to the same limit SSS. ■\blacksquare■

So ∑kk+1\sum \frac{k}{k+1}∑k+1k​ diverges, since its terms tend to 111. The converse is false, and the harmonic series is the standard counterexample.

The harmonic series diverges

Theorem. ∑k=1∞1k\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac1k∑k=1∞​k1​ diverges, although 1k→0\frac1k \to 0k1​→0.

Proof. Group the terms in blocks that end at powers of 222:

s2m=1+12+(13+14)+(15+⋯+18)+⋯+(12m−1+1+⋯+12m).s_{2^m} = 1 + \tfrac12 + \left(\tfrac13 + \tfrac14\right) + \left(\tfrac15 + \cdots + \tfrac18\right) + \cdots + \left(\tfrac{1}{2^{m-1}+1} + \cdots + \tfrac{1}{2^m}\right). s2m​=1+21​+(31​+41​)+(51​+⋯+81​)+⋯+(2m−1+11​+⋯+2m1​).

Each bracket has 2j−12^{j-1}2j−1 terms, each at least 12j\frac{1}{2^j}2j1​, so each bracket is at least 12\frac1221​. Hence s2m≥1+m2s_{2^m} \ge 1 + \frac{m}{2}s2m​≥1+2m​. The partial sums are increasing and unbounded, so the series diverges. ■\blacksquare■

The actual values confirm the bound: s2=1.5s_2 = 1.5s2​=1.5, s4≈2.083s_4 \approx 2.083s4​≈2.083, s8≈2.718s_8 \approx 2.718s8​≈2.718, s16≈3.381s_{16} \approx 3.381s16​≈3.381, s32≈4.058s_{32} \approx 4.058s32​≈4.058, each at least 1+m/21 + m/21+m/2. The growth is very slow — sns_nsn​ grows like ln⁡n\ln nlnn.

The Cauchy criterion for series

Applying the Cauchy criterion to (sn)(s_n)(sn​): ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges if and only if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is NNN such that for all n>m≥Nn > m \ge Nn>m≥N,

∣am+1+am+2+⋯+an∣<ε.\lvert a_{m+1} + a_{m+2} + \cdots + a_n \rvert < \varepsilon. ∣am+1​+am+2​+⋯+an​∣<ε.

"The blocks far out add up to almost nothing." The harmonic series fails this: the block from m+1m+1m+1 to 2m2m2m is always at least m⋅12m=12m \cdot \frac{1}{2m} = \frac12m⋅2m1​=21​.

Chapter 6 — Convergence tests

Comparison

Comparison test. Suppose 0≤ak≤bk0 \le a_k \le b_k0≤ak​≤bk​ for all kkk.
(i) If ∑bk\sum b_k∑bk​ converges, so does ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​.
(ii) If ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ diverges, so does ∑bk\sum b_k∑bk​.

Proof. The partial sums of ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ are increasing and bounded by ∑bk\sum b_k∑bk​; apply the Monotone Convergence Theorem. Part (ii) is the contrapositive of (i). ■\blacksquare■

Example: ∑1/k2\sum 1/k^2∑1/k2 converges. For k≥2k \ge 2k≥2, 1k2<1k(k−1)=1k−1−1k\frac{1}{k^2} < \frac{1}{k(k-1)} = \frac{1}{k-1} - \frac1kk21​<k(k−1)1​=k−11​−k1​, a telescoping series with sum 111. So ∑k=1∞1k2<1+1=2\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k^2} < 1 + 1 = 2∑k=1∞​k21​<1+1=2 converges. (Its exact value, π2/6≈1.645\pi^2/6 \approx 1.645π2/6≈1.645, is Euler's solution of the Basel problem.)

ppp-series. ∑1kp\sum \frac{1}{k^p}∑kp1​ converges if and only if p>1p > 1p>1. (Cauchy condensation or the integral test, Abbott Section 2.4.)

Ratio and root tests

Ratio test. Suppose ak≠0a_k \ne 0ak​=0 and lim⁡∣ak+1ak∣=r\lim \left\lvert \frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k} \right\rvert = rlim​ak​ak+1​​​=r. If r<1r < 1r<1, ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges absolutely; if r>1r > 1r>1, it diverges; if r=1r = 1r=1, the test says nothing.

Root test. Let r=lim sup⁡∣ak∣1/kr = \limsup \lvert a_k \rvert^{1/k}r=limsup∣ak​∣1/k. If r<1r < 1r<1, ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges absolutely; if r>1r > 1r>1, it diverges; if r=1r = 1r=1, no conclusion.

Both tests compare with a geometric series: if r<1r < 1r<1, pick qqq with r<q<1r < q < 1r<q<1; eventually ∣ak∣≤Cqk\lvert a_k \rvert \le C q^k∣ak​∣≤Cqk.

Example. ∑k=1∞k2k\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{k}{2^k}∑k=1∞​2kk​: ak+1ak=k+12k→12<1\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k} = \frac{k+1}{2k} \to \frac12 < 1ak​ak+1​​=2kk+1​→21​<1, so it converges. (Its sum is 222.)

Watch out: r=1r = 1r=1 is genuinely inconclusive. Both ∑1/k\sum 1/k∑1/k (divergent) and ∑1/k2\sum 1/k^2∑1/k2 (convergent) have ratio limit 111.

Alternating series

Alternating Series Test. If (ak)(a_k)(ak​) is decreasing and ak→0a_k \to 0ak​→0, then ∑k=1∞(−1)k+1ak=a1−a2+a3−⋯\sum_{k=1}^\infty (-1)^{k+1} a_k = a_1 - a_2 + a_3 - \cdots∑k=1∞​(−1)k+1ak​=a1​−a2​+a3​−⋯ converges.

Proof sketch. The even partial sums s2n=(a1−a2)+⋯+(a2n−1−a2n)s_{2n} = (a_1 - a_2) + \cdots + (a_{2n-1} - a_{2n})s2n​=(a1​−a2​)+⋯+(a2n−1​−a2n​) increase; the odd ones s2n+1=a1−(a2−a3)−⋯s_{2n+1} = a_1 - (a_2 - a_3) - \cdotss2n+1​=a1​−(a2​−a3​)−⋯ decrease; and s2n≤s2n+1s_{2n} \le s_{2n+1}s2n​≤s2n+1​ with s2n+1−s2n=a2n+1→0s_{2n+1} - s_{2n} = a_{2n+1} \to 0s2n+1​−s2n​=a2n+1​→0. So the intervals [s2n,s2n+1][s_{2n}, s_{2n+1}][s2n​,s2n+1​] are nested with lengths going to 000, and all partial sums converge to the single common point. ■\blacksquare■

The proof also gives the error bound: the sum lies between any two consecutive partial sums, so ∣S−sn∣≤an+1\lvert S - s_n \rvert \le a_{n+1}∣S−sn​∣≤an+1​.

Example. The alternating harmonic series converges:

1−12+13−14+⋯=ln⁡2≈0.6931.1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \frac14 + \cdots = \ln 2 \approx 0.6931. 1−21​+31​−41​+⋯=ln2≈0.6931.

(The value ln⁡2\ln 2ln2 comes from the Taylor series of ln⁡(1+x)\ln(1 + x)ln(1+x) evaluated at x=1x = 1x=1; the test itself gives only convergence.)

Absolute and conditional convergence

  • ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges absolutely if ∑∣ak∣\sum \lvert a_k \rvert∑∣ak​∣ converges.
  • It converges conditionally if it converges but ∑∣ak∣\sum \lvert a_k \rvert∑∣ak​∣ diverges.

Theorem. Absolute convergence implies convergence.

Proof. By the triangle inequality ∣am+1+⋯+an∣≤∣am+1∣+⋯+∣an∣\lvert a_{m+1} + \cdots + a_n \rvert \le \lvert a_{m+1} \rvert + \cdots + \lvert a_n \rvert∣am+1​+⋯+an​∣≤∣am+1​∣+⋯+∣an​∣. If ∑∣ak∣\sum \lvert a_k \rvert∑∣ak​∣ satisfies the Cauchy criterion, so does ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​. ■\blacksquare■

The alternating harmonic series converges conditionally: it converges, but ∑1k\sum \frac1k∑k1​ diverges.

Rearrangements

A rearrangement of ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ is ∑af(k)\sum a_{f(k)}∑af(k)​ for a bijection f:N→Nf : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}f:N→N — the same terms in a different order.

Theorem. If ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges absolutely, every rearrangement converges to the same sum.

Riemann rearrangement theorem. If ∑ak\sum a_k∑ak​ converges conditionally, then for every L∈RL \in \mathbb{R}L∈R there is a rearrangement that converges to LLL (and there are rearrangements that diverge).

The idea: the positive terms alone and the negative terms alone both diverge. Add positive terms until you pass LLL, then negative terms until you drop below LLL, and repeat; since ak→0a_k \to 0ak​→0, the overshoots shrink to 000.

Example. Rearrange the alternating harmonic series as "one positive term, then two negative terms":

1−12−14+13−16−18+15−110−112+⋯1 - \frac12 - \frac14 + \frac13 - \frac16 - \frac18 + \frac15 - \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{12} + \cdots 1−21​−41​+31​−61​−81​+51​−101​−121​+⋯

Group each block of three. Since 12k−1−14k−2=14k−2\frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{4k-2} = \frac{1}{4k-2}2k−11​−4k−21​=4k−21​, the kkk-th block is

14k−2−14k=12(12k−1−12k).\frac{1}{4k-2} - \frac{1}{4k} = \frac12 \left( \frac{1}{2k-1} - \frac{1}{2k} \right). 4k−21​−4k1​=21​(2k−11​−2k1​).

So the block sums add up to half of the alternating harmonic series: the rearranged series converges to 12ln⁡2\tfrac12 \ln 221​ln2, not ln⁡2\ln 2ln2. (The partial sums that stop inside a block differ from the block sums by terms tending to 000, so they have the same limit.)

Common pitfall: treating an infinite sum like a finite one. Regrouping, reordering and term-by-term manipulations are safe for absolutely convergent series, and can fail for conditionally convergent ones.

Practice Exercises

1. Prove from the definition that 3n−1n+2→3\frac{3n - 1}{n + 2} \to 3n+23n−1​→3. Find the smallest valid NNN for ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1.

Solution

∣3n−1n+2−3∣=7n+2\left\lvert \frac{3n-1}{n+2} - 3 \right\rvert = \frac{7}{n+2}​n+23n−1​−3​=n+27​. Given ε\varepsilonε, choose N>7/ε−2N > 7/\varepsilon - 2N>7/ε−2; then for n≥Nn \ge Nn≥N, 7n+2≤7N+2<ε\frac{7}{n+2} \le \frac{7}{N+2} < \varepsilonn+27​≤N+27​<ε. For ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 the condition is n>68n > 68n>68, so the smallest NNN is 696969 (at n=68n = 68n=68 the distance is 770=0.1\frac{7}{70} = 0.1707​=0.1 exactly, which is not <0.1< 0.1<0.1).

Solution

By the reverse triangle inequality, ∣∣an∣−∣a∣∣≤∣an−a∣\big\lvert \lvert a_n \rvert - \lvert a \rvert \big\rvert \le \lvert a_n - a \rvert​∣an​∣−∣a∣​≤∣an​−a∣, so the same NNN works. The converse is false: an=(−1)na_n = (-1)^nan​=(−1)n has ∣an∣→1\lvert a_n \rvert \to 1∣an​∣→1 but diverges. (It is true when a=0a = 0a=0.)

3. Let x1=3x_1 = 3x1​=3 and xn+1=12xn+1x_{n+1} = \frac12 x_n + 1xn+1​=21​xn​+1. Prove that (xn)(x_n)(xn​) converges and find its limit.

Solution

Claim: xn>2x_n > 2xn​>2 and decreasing. If xn>2x_n > 2xn​>2 then xn+1=12xn+1>2x_{n+1} = \frac12 x_n + 1 > 2xn+1​=21​xn​+1>2. And xn−xn+1=12xn−1=12(xn−2)>0x_n - x_{n+1} = \frac12 x_n - 1 = \frac12(x_n - 2) > 0xn​−xn+1​=21​xn​−1=21​(xn​−2)>0. So (xn)(x_n)(xn​) is decreasing and bounded below by 222, hence converges to some LLL. Taking limits in the recursion: L=12L+1L = \frac12 L + 1L=21​L+1, so L=2L = 2L=2. (Terms: 3,2.5,2.25,2.125,…3, 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, \dots3,2.5,2.25,2.125,…; in fact xn=2+21−nx_n = 2 + 2^{1-n}xn​=2+21−n.)

4. Use subsequences to show that an=cos⁡(nπ2)a_n = \cos\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)an​=cos(2nπ​) diverges, and find its lim sup⁡\limsuplimsup and lim inf⁡\liminfliminf.

The terms cycle 0,−1,0,1,…0, -1, 0, 1, \dots0,−1,0,1,… (for n=1,2,3,4,…n = 1, 2, 3, 4, \dotsn=1,2,3,4,…). The subsequence a4k=1→1a_{4k} = 1 \to 1a4k​=1→1 and a4k+2=−1→−1a_{4k+2} = -1 \to -1a4k+2​=−1→−1 have different limits, so (an)(a_n)(an​) diverges. 5. Decide whether each series converges: (a) ∑12k+k\sum \frac{1}{2^k + k}∑2k+k1​; (b) ∑k23k\sum \frac{k^2}{3^k}∑3kk2​; (c) ∑1k\sum \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}∑k​1​; (d) ∑(−1)k1k\sum (-1)^k \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}∑(−1)kk​1​.

Solution

(a) Converges: 0<12k+k<12k0 < \frac{1}{2^k + k} < \frac{1}{2^k}0<2k+k1​<2k1​, a convergent geometric series. (b) Converges by the ratio test: (k+1)23k2→13<1\frac{(k+1)^2}{3k^2} \to \frac13 < 13k2(k+1)2​→31​<1. (c) Diverges: 1k≥1k\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}} \ge \frac1kk​1​≥k1​ and the harmonic series diverges. 6. Show that ∑k=1∞1k(k+2)=34\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k(k+2)} = \frac34∑k=1∞​k(k+2)1​=43​.

Solution

1k(k+2)=12(1k−1k+2)\frac{1}{k(k+2)} = \frac12\left(\frac1k - \frac{1}{k+2}\right)k(k+2)1​=21​(k1​−k+21​). The partial sum telescopes, leaving the first two positive and last two negative terms: sn=12(1+12−1n+1−1n+2)→12⋅32=34s_n = \frac12\left(1 + \frac12 - \frac{1}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+2}\right) \to \frac12 \cdot \frac32 = \frac34sn​=21​(1+21​−n+11​−n+21​)→21​⋅23​=43​.

7. Give an example of a bounded sequence with no convergent subsequence, or explain why none exists. Then give an unbounded sequence with a convergent subsequence.

Solution

None exists: Bolzano–Weierstrass says every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. An unbounded example: an=na_n = nan​=n for odd nnn and an=0a_n = 0an​=0 for even nnn; the even terms form a constant, convergent subsequence.

What's next

Real Analysis 02 moves from sequences to sets and functions: open and closed sets, compactness (where Bolzano–Weierstrass becomes Heine–Borel), limits of functions via the ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ definition and its sequential form, continuity, the Extreme and Intermediate Value Theorems, and uniform continuity.

References

  • Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis, 2nd edition, Springer, 2015 — Chapter 2 (sequences and series), Section 2.7 (rearrangements).
  • Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd edition, McGraw-Hill, 1976 — Chapter 3 (numerical sequences and series; Theorem 3.54 is Riemann's theorem).
  • Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis, 4th edition, Wiley, 2011 — Chapter 3 (sequences, including the number eee) and Chapter 9 (infinite series).
  • Terence Tao, Analysis I, 4th edition, Springer, 2022 — Chapters 6–7.
  • Konrad Knopp, Theory and Application of Infinite Series, Dover reprint, 1990 — the classic reference for convergence tests.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.100A Real Analysis, Fall 2020 (Casey Rodriguez), lecture notes: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-100a-real-analysis-fall-2020/

Note: this post is in progress. Planned additions: full proofs of the quotient rule for limits and of the ratio and root tests; Cauchy condensation; and the proof of the Riemann rearrangement theorem.
